drills.coachNote: White's rook on b6, backed by the c5-d6-e6 pawns, wants Rb8+, and the d6 pawn is already eyeing your knight on e7. Kd8 walks straight into that: Rb8+, Nc8, c6, and your knight is boxed in while Rh7 mops up your rook on h8 — your winning position collapses. Kc8 keeps your king near c7/b7, so after c6 you have Bc4 hitting the rook first; White still wins the knight with dxe7, but your king stays active and you hold the balance instead of losing outright. When a rook and passed pawns threaten your back rank, choose the king square that keeps you connected.

drills.coachNote: You're completely winning here, and White's only lifeline is getting his knight on b1 into play — Nd2 followed by Qc2 is how he untangles. Rxb2 grabs a pawn but hands him exactly that tempo: after Nd2, Qc2, Rh2 he's consolidating and even nibbling back your d3 pawn, turning a forced mate into a mere endgame edge. Qg2 is mate on the spot instead — your queen lands on g2 defended by your rook on f2, and the king on g1 has nowhere to go, with h1, h2 and f1 all covered. When the enemy king is this boxed in, scan for the finishing blow before you cash in material.

drills.coachNote: In this kind of pawn ending, Black's only resource is to shuffle the king opposite yours and deny you a free tempo to break through. Kf4 looks natural but gains nothing concrete — after Kf7, e4, Ke7, Ke3 you're back in the same standoff, and having committed your king to f4 first, you gave Black's king the tempo to mirror you, which is why a +19.8 position got far messier than it needed to. Kf3 keeps your king centralized without committing early, so when you do play e4, your king, the bishop on c4, and the c6/e5/g5 pawns are already coordinated. In king-and-pawn endings, don't send your king forward until you're sure the move improves your winning try.

Bb3 sits on the same a2-g8 diagonal as Bc4, so it changes nothing; it's a wasted tempo. The engine line shows that after Bb3, Ke7, Kc4, Black gets back to f7, and you still have to play Ba2 anyway — a move later than needed. Ba2 goes straight to the useful square so your king can start marching immediately: Kc4-Kb5, squeezing Black's king before it can regroup. In dead-won endgames, spend every move on progress.

Ra7 solves it directly: the rook parks behind the a-pawn on its own file, freezing it, while your king marches in with Kd6 and you pick up tempo later with Rg8+.
